focus: Validated the Phase 1 admin_init anomalies against the real callback bodies and their write sinks.
Traced the featured-image save, REST meta, and AJAX toggle surfaces to determine whether any low-privileged actor can modify meaningful state.
Reviewed the SVG upload, REST upload, file read/write, remote fetch, and frontend inline-rendering paths for Patchstack-relevant XSS, SSRF, and arbitrary file operation impact.
analysis_summary.result: No Patchstack-eligible true positive was confirmed in SVG Support 2.5.14 after direct source validation.
analysis_summary.key_observation: The interesting surfaces are either fixed migration/helpers with no attacker-controlled input, or they stay inside normal WordPress post-edit and upload capability boundaries. The packaged plugin does expose several configuration footguns, but not a default low-privilege exploit path.
tooling_notes: Phase 1 IR and Semgrep were used as signal sources only.

negative_findings.title: admin_init anomalies are fixed migrations or UI helpers, not request-driven privilege breaks

evidence.note: bodhi_svgs_register_settings() only calls register_setting() with a sanitize callback.
bodhi_svgs_remove_old_sanitize_setting() reads the fixed bodhi_svgs_settings option and removes one legacy key before update_option().
bodhi_svgs_display_thumbs() only installs output-buffer helpers for the media-library UI template.
bodhi_svgs_version_updates() compares a fixed version option and, on upgrade, runs a local cleanup helper.
The cleanup SQL uses only hard-coded meta_key = 'inline_featured_image'; no request input reaches the query.

reasoning.hypothesis: Missing nonce and capability checks on admin_init might let subscriber-level users force privileged option or database writes.
reasoning.trace: The reviewed admin_init callbacks register plugin settings, remove one obsolete array key from bodhi_svgs_settings, patch the media-library template output, or migrate duplicate inline_featured_image meta during a version bump.
reasoning.defenses: None of the reviewed callbacks read $_GET, $_POST, $_REQUEST, or any other user-controlled parameter before reaching update_option() or $wpdb->query(). The write targets are fixed plugin-owned keys and fixed SQL conditions.
reasoning.refutation: I did not find any attacker-controlled source flowing into these sinks. A low-privileged user can trigger admin_init, but they cannot influence the migrated values, the option key, or the SQL predicates. The resulting side effects are maintenance-only and do not cross a security boundary.
reasoning.conclusion: Rejected as a false positive. Phase 1 correctly noticed missing guards, but the reachable sinks are not request-driven and do not create measurable security impact.

negative_findings.reopen_if: Show a bundled request parameter or lower-privileged UI flow that lets an attacker influence the data written by these admin_init callbacks.

negative_findings.title: Featured-image meta surfaces do not produce a practical low-privileged write primitive

evidence.note: Classic-editor save path verifies bodhi_svgs_featured_image_nonce before any meta write.
Classic-editor save path also enforces current_user_can('edit_post', $post_id).
The registered meta is a boolean flag named inline_featured_image that is exposed to REST.
The shipped block-editor UI updates inline_featured_image through core/editor.editPost({ meta }), not through the custom AJAX action.
The custom AJAX handler requires wp_verify_nonce(..., 'svg-support-featured') and then current_user_can('edit_posts') before add_post_meta().
Both logged-in and nopriv AJAX hooks point to the same handler.
Repo-wide search found the svg-support-featured nonce string only in this handler; no bundled wp_create_nonce() or client caller was found.

reasoning.hypothesis: The nopriv AJAX registration and the weak current_user_can('edit_posts') check could let low-privileged or unauthenticated users toggle inline_featured_image for arbitrary posts.
reasoning.trace: The real storage key is inline_featured_image. In the classic editor, it is written through save_post only after a post-specific nonce and current_user_can('edit_post', $post_id). In Gutenberg, the packaged UI edits the same boolean meta through the normal post-save flow. The custom AJAX route exists, but it first requires a svg-support-featured nonce, then requires current_user_can('edit_posts'), and only writes the same boolean flag via bodhi_svgs_update_featured_image_meta().
reasoning.defenses: The nopriv hook still fails current_user_can('edit_posts') for user 0. The packaged plugin does not mint or localize the svg-support-featured nonce anywhere else, so I did not find a working caller for the custom AJAX route. The affected storage key only toggles whether a featured SVG is rendered inline.
reasoning.refutation: I found no bundled source for a valid svg-support-featured nonce, and no shipped JavaScript calls the AJAX action. Even if an editor-level user could somehow reach the sink, the only writable state is the inline_featured_image boolean, which does not grant privileges, disclose data, or control an attacker-chosen option key.
reasoning.conclusion: Rejected as a false positive. The noisy AJAX registration and permissive auth_callback do not become a Patchstack-relevant exploit path in the packaged plugin.

negative_findings.reopen_if: Show a bundled low-privileged surface that emits a valid svg-support-featured nonce, or demonstrate that writing inline_featured_image for another post yields a concrete security impact beyond presentation changes.

negative_findings.title: SVG upload and REST upload paths did not yield a low-privilege sanitization bypass or arbitrary file write

evidence.note: SVG MIME support is only added when the current user's role is in the configured allowlist and current_user_can('upload_files') succeeds.
bodhi_svgs_sanitize_svg() validates extension, MIME, and SVG structure before any write-back.
Non-REST uploads also require a valid media-form nonce.
The prefilter sanitizes the temporary upload unless the current role is explicitly configured to bypass sanitization.
bodhi_svgs_sanitize() constrains tags and attributes, removes remote references, and writes the sanitized SVG back to the same temp file.
REST uploads get an additional rest_pre_upload_file sanitization pass.
rest_insert_attachment() can re-sanitize the stored SVG file after insertion for the same REST path.

reasoning.hypothesis: A subscriber or other low-privileged actor may be able to upload an unsanitized SVG or steer the file_get_contents()/file_put_contents() calls in attachment.php toward arbitrary files.
reasoning.trace: Before WordPress accepts an SVG upload, the plugin must first add SVG to the caller's allowed MIME types, which only happens for configured roles that also have upload_files. The prefilter then validates MIME and content, rejects malformed SVGs, and sanitizes the current temporary upload file. REST uploads take the same upload path and also hit rest_pre_upload_file() and, later, rest_insert_attachment().
reasoning.defenses: Role allowlist, current_user_can('upload_files'), MIME/content validation, enshrined/svg-sanitize allowlists, removeRemoteReferences(true), and repeated REST-specific sanitization passes all sit before or around the write sinks.
reasoning.refutation: I did not find a source-to-sink path from subscriber or unauthenticated input to file_put_contents() outside the current upload temp file already under WordPress's upload transaction. The strict content-type check in rest_insert_attachment() is not a practical bypass because wp_handle_upload_prefilter() already sanitizes .svg uploads earlier in the same flow.
reasoning.conclusion: Rejected as a false positive. The file read/write sinks in attachment.php stay inside the expected WordPress upload boundary and do not form a low-privilege arbitrary write or stored-XSS primitive in the packaged plugin.

negative_findings.reopen_if: Show a bundled low-privileged role that can upload SVGs without passing through bodhi_svgs_sanitize_svg(), or a path that redirects the read/write sinks away from the current upload temp file.

negative_findings.title: Remote fetch and XML parsing in attachment metadata are not a practical SSRF or XXE sink here

evidence.note: wp_prepare_attachment_for_js only falls back to a URL when get_attached_file() no longer resolves to a local path for an existing attachment.
bodhi_svgs_get_dimensions() calls wp_remote_get() only when it is handed a URL, otherwise it reads the local attachment file.
simplexml_load_string() is called without LIBXML_NOENT, LIBXML_DTDLOAD, or other entity-expansion flags.
Metadata generation passes get_attached_file($attachment_id) back into bodhi_svgs_get_dimensions().

reasoning.hypothesis: The remote wp_remote_get() and simplexml_load_string() calls might let a low-privileged user trigger SSRF or XXE through a crafted SVG or attachment URL.
reasoning.trace: The reviewed call sites derive their input from existing WordPress attachment data: either get_attached_file($attachment->ID) or the already-stored attachment response URL when the local file is missing. The packaged plugin's upload flow stores local uploads and does not expose a route for lower-privileged users to create arbitrary external attachment URLs.
reasoning.defenses: No bundled source lets a lower-privileged user choose the URL passed into wp_remote_get(). The XML parser is invoked without entity-expansion flags, and a local PHP 8.5 CLI check with external file and HTTP entities returned empty text rather than resolving the entity in this environment.
reasoning.refutation: I found no packaged low-privilege entry point that can set an arbitrary remote attachment URL or a controlled filesystem path before these sinks execute. I also could not reproduce default external-entity expansion in the local environment.
reasoning.conclusion: Rejected as a false positive for this plugin package. The code is worth hardening, but I do not have a source-to-sink exploit path with practical low-privileged impact.

negative_findings.reopen_if: Show a bundled path that lets a low-privileged user set an attachment URL to an attacker-controlled remote host, or reproduce entity expansion on a supported PHP/WordPress target without additional libxml flags.

out_of_scope.title: Admin-configurable unsanitized SVG modes can reintroduce XSS risk in downstream deployments
out_of_scope.auth_required: administrator to weaken the default configuration; lower-role exploitability depends on that change

evidence.note: The plugin defaults to sanitize_svg_front_end = on, restrict = ['administrator'], and sanitize_on_upload_roles = [].
The settings page lets administrators widen SVG upload eligibility, exempt chosen roles from sanitization, and disable front-end sanitization.
Uploads bypass sanitization when the current role intersects sanitize_on_upload_roles.
DOMPurify is only enqueued when sanitize_svg_front_end is on and advanced mode is enabled.
When frontSanitizationEnabled is off, the inline renderer replaces the IMG tag with raw fetched SVG markup.

out_of_scope.reasoning: This is not a packaged vulnerability because the default posture is defensive and any weaker behavior requires an administrator to deliberately loosen the role and sanitization settings. If a site owner both grants SVG upload capability to weaker roles and disables or bypasses sanitization, inline rendering can become an XSS footgun. That is a deployment choice rather than a default low-privilege exploit path in the shipped plugin.
